speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INDO-CHINA-REPORTED INABILITY OF TRUCE COMMISSION TO OPERATE
speechtext:
Last Friday the hon. member for Prince Albert asked a question concerning freedom of movement in North Viet


Nam, a matter which has aroused very considerable interest throughout the country, and I should like to make a statement on it now, Mr. Speaker.
The situation with respect to freedom of movement for refugees from Viet Nam, which was provided for under article 14(d) of the armistice agreement, is not satisfactory, nor does the international supervisory commission regard it as so; certainly the Canadian member on that commission does not.
The commission announced early in February last that it had found that the procedure to ensure this movement by the issue of travel permits was cumbrous and complicated, and that fears current among the population in North Viet Nam had tended to make them reluctant to apply to the authorities for such permits. Action was taken by the commission which it was hoped would facilitate the proper and more effective implementation of this part of the agreement. However, reports to the effect that people in North Viet Nam were still being prevented from exercising their rights of freedom of movement have persisted. Therefore the international commission recently sent three further mobile teams, on each of which of course there was a Canadian, to make a special survey of those areas in North Viet Nam concerning which complaints had been made. On the basis of the reports of this survey, the commission is now determining what further action is necessary.
There are, Mr. Speaker, of course, limitations on the effectiveness of international inspection by the commission in this and in other matters. Some of these limitations are inherent in the cease-fire agreement itself. It reflects the fact that the commission is not a supra-national body, that it does not have any executive responsibilities with respect to the carrying out of the agreement and that its inspection teams do not in any sense constitute international police detachments. The commission can only operate with the effective co-operation of the parties to the agreement and it does not always receive that co-operation, especially in this question of freedom of movement, from the communist government in North Viet Nam, and that is the main reason why in this matter the results have been disappointing, to say the least.
I would not wish anyone to think that our representatives on the international commission for Viet Nam are satisfied with the way the freedom of movement provisions of the armistice agreement are being carried out. They are not satisfied, and the government fully shares that dissatisfaction. Our Views have been stated very clearly in the

international commission in Viet Nam, and have, I think, had some effect on the decisions of the commission.
If one of the parties to the agreement is evading its clear obligations and responsibilities with respect to the freedom of movement for civilians, it is not going unnoticed by our representative on the commission or by the government. But this is not a situation, I suggest, which will be solved merely by letting off steam. We are convinced that in order to ensure that the provisions of the agreement are carried out to the greatest degree possible in the circumstances, we must continue to work through our representative on the commission in the same manner as we have done over the last eight months, pressing for better performance in every way possible and exposing violations when they can be detected. That still seems to us to be the most likely method of ensuring that the greatest possible number of people who wish to do so can leave North Viet Nam for the south.
There have been suggestions in some quarters that Canada might withdraw from the commission as a gesture of protest about the way the commission has been prevented from correcting the situation with respect to freedom of movement. Such a move would, however, prejudice also the fulfilment of the main military provisions of the agreement, thus creating new tensions and possibly jeopardizing the maintenance of peace, not only in Viet Nam but also in the neighbouring countries of Laos and Cambodia. Nor would our withdrawal be of any assistance whatsoever to those in North Viet Nam who want to leave. Indeed, It might eliminate any remaining hope that their lot might be alleviated. We must, therefore, keep our sense of perspective in this matter, but without condoning or forgetting some of the terrible things that are being done.
A question was asked also by the hon. member for Prince Albert the other day as to the possibility that the time for freedom of movement for refugees might be extended beyond the terminal date, which is May 18, I think. The commission is actively concerned with finding ways and means of ensuring that this provision of the cease-fire agreement is properly implemented, and it will, I am sure, consider the possibility of an extension, if necessary; but any extension of the period would require the concurrence of both parties to the cease-fire agreement, whose full co-operation would be required if an extension were to provide a real solution to the problem.
I tabled today, Mr. Speaker, copies of the first interim reports of the commission for
Inquiries of the Ministry Viet Nam and the second interim report. But I should like to point out now and emphasize that the reports of the commission were in each case prepared by the commission as a whole, including the Polish and Indian members as well as the Canadian representative. It may be that these reports, therefore, do not reflect entirely our dissatisfaction with the freedom of movement position.
I understand that the Viet Nam commission has recently completed a third interim report which is now being forwarded to the Geneva conference powers, as indeed the first two have been. In connection with the submission of this report, steps have been taken by the Canadian representative to ensure that the unsatisfactory situation with respect to the carrying out of the provisions in the agreement for freedom of movement for the civil population will be given special attention.

Has he noted in an article by Ainslie Kerr the following matters as examples of flagrant breaches of the agreement, and does he know whether or not these examples are actually correct in fact? The first is, is it a fact that communist Viet Nam guards have made Indian committee members surrender, at bayonet point, documents handed to them by the inhabitants of North Viet Nam who had prepared those documents in pursuance of the Geneva agreement? Is it so that masses of military equipment and red troops are pouring into Viet Nam contrary to the agreements that were entered into at the time of the truce? Is it so that even our Canadian inspection teams are denied the opportunity to inspect without first giving notice, thereby denying anything in the nature of factual inspection? speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INDO-CHINA-REPORTED INABILITY OF TRUCE COMMISSION TO OPERATE
speechtext:
I am not able to confirm in all its detail the accuracy of the report to which my hon. friend has referred. We are trying to get specific information from Viet Nam on these three points. However, I think I can say that it is probably an exaggeration to indicate that Chinese troops are pouring into Viet Nam across the borders. Reports cannot be entirely conclusive in these matters because of the nature of the situation, but there is nothing in the reports we have received which would warrant that conclusion.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I have said already that there is an unsatisfactory situation with regard to freedom of movement, but that is as far as I can go in regard to details.
So far as the other question is concerned, when any complaint comes to the attention of the commission or to the attention of our representative on the commission he makes his position clear to the other members. Very often as a result of the attitude taken by our member or by some other member of the commission steps are taken to correct a situation, but the government on the spot in North Viet Nam has the responsibility of taking the actual executive remedial action. Of course there is difficulty at times in ensuring that that is done.
I do not know that I can go beyond that. Our member on the commission has to work with the other members. Naturally we hope that the commission will act unanimously in all these matters. While we do make our position known and when a complaint is justified we make a complaint; nevertheless we do try to work with the other two members of the commission.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I was referring to the Chignecto canal and I should like to complete my remarks on that subject. Before I do so I should like to bring to the attention of the house something I have read since last evening of the third annual report of the Colombo plan. On page 119 the following appears:
The Canadian parliament voted $25-4 million for use under the Colombo plan in 1954-55, making a total of approximately $102 million which has been made available by Canada for capital and technical assistance in the first four years of the plan.
And then on the following page, under "India":
6. Some parts of the 1954-55 program for India are still under discussion. However, to date India has been allocated approximately $49 million in Colombo plan assistance from Canada.
8. Another project which is to be assisted by Canada is the Umtru hydro-electric scheme in Assam. Canada will provide electrical equipment to an estimated amount of $1-2 million.
10.	Other projects in India are being examined by the Canadian authorities, including the possibility of supplying a number of small thermal power units for use in a number of communities spread widely throughout India.
And then under "Pakistan":
11.	However, to date Pakistan has been allocated a total of approximately $33 million in Colombo plan assistance from Canada.
12.	As mentioned in the 1953 report Canada has undertaken to participate in the construction of the Warsak dam in northwest Pakistan. Up to the present $5-4 million has been earmarked for the purchase of hydro-electric and related equipment.
Under "Ceylon", on page 122, I find in item 17:
To assist in the development of the port of Colombo, electrical and other equipment up to a value of $400,000 will be supplied by Canada.
On page 48 of this report I find mention made of several projects. One is the Nangal dam and the Nangal canal. Also mentioned is the Kakrapara canal system.
I thought that this was an opportune time to bring to the attention of this house the Canadian money that is being spent under the Colombo plan for the development in India, Pakistan and Ceylon of canals and dams, similar to what we are asking for in New Brunswick. I feel that we in New Brunswick are as worthy of assistance as anybody outside of Canada, and we should be given the same break as the people of India, Pakistan and Ceylon. At least, we should be regarded as a friendly country.
If you will look at a map of the sea lanes, you will find sea lanes coming out of the
The Budget-Mr. H. J. Murphy St. Lawrence river and going around the maritime provinces to the ports of New York and Boston and the cities farther south. To say that the St. Lawrence seaway will not benefit the province of New Brunswick is in my opinion true, and especially in my own constituency of Westmorland, where the Canadian National Railways shops and offices are located. That may mean a lessening of rail traffic, because in the wintertime and even at other times of the year a considerable volume of goods is shipped from western Canada and the central provinces to Halifax and Saint John by rail. It is in the interests of Canada, and we accept the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway should be built, but I do not think that the applause for building this seaway should be so loud that notice should not be taken or arguments heard for the continuance of the seaway by building the Chignecto canal.
In case there are some hon. members who are not familiar with the geography of the maritime provinces, I want to tell you that the province of Nova Scotia is connected with the province of New Brunswick by the isthmus of Chignecto. This isthmus is 18 miles wide and separates Northumberland strait from the bay of Fundy, so that a ship coming out of the St. Lawrence seaway through Northumberland strait must go around the entire province of Nova Scotia, an additional distance of 500 miles, to reach the ports of the eastern seaboard. Another matter which occurs to me is the part that is to be played by the United States in the construction of this seaway. I have often heard it said, "Let us be fair". Then let us be fair to the Americans. We should complete the seaway by the construction of this canal so that, after they have paid for so much of the cost of the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, they will not be cut off from the use of their eastern ports by the isthmus of Chignecto. If this isthmus were pierced by a canal, the ships from Chignecto could go to New York through Chignecto with their loads of grain and continue to South America, discharging or taking on cargoes in passing. It seems to me that, as far as use by the ports of Portland, Boston and New York of the St. Lawrence seaway is concerned, such use will be very limited. The St. Lawrence seaway has been put over on the Americans in that they did not insist on the construction of the Chignecto canal.
This year there will be a ferry running from Yarmouth to Portland, and I understand that this ferry will be able to carry approximately 150 cars. The trip from Yarmouth to Portland is 700 miles by land; by sea, I understand, it is somewhat less than

The Budget~Mr. Fleming 200 miles. Now, the people of Yarmouth and that part of Nova Scotia near it are going to have the advantages of shipping their produce to the markets of New England by the use of this ferry from Yarmouth to Portland, but the people on the north side of the isthmus, along the northern coast of Nova Scotia, the eastern coast of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, are being denied the use of the sea route to the United States ports by the failure to build the Chignecto canal.
I have spoken in this house every time I have got the chance about the Chignecto canal and, to tell you the truth, I have not got much further ahead than when I started with the process of construction. So I was going to ask that this house institute an investigation, a survey, a commission, or some board, to look into all the aspects of the construction of the Chignecto canal so that we will know once and for all whether or not we can look forward in the near future to the construction of this canal, and by the same token we will know what our economic possibilities are in New Brunswick.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the presentation of the budget provides one of the annual dramas in the House of Commons. We have few of them indeed in a normal session of parliament, and we all look forward to the presentation of the budget. The task that falls to the opposition following the presentation of that budget is not always a dramatic one, but it is a highly important one in relation to the whole purpose of our parliamentary institutions. In no particular of its responsibilities in any normal session does the opposition rise to a higher duty than in relation to the examination of the government's budget.
It is true that in the house, constituted as this one is at present, the government wins the vote. But it is equally true that in relation to the kind of budget we are discussing here today the opposition wins the debate. But what of the people? The Canadian people from this budget will glean but little benefit, but they will glean something of benefit from the debate in which the proposals of the government are examined.
I wish to be fair to the minister. This is his first budget, and one would of course wish to congratulate him upon the opportunity of presenting the budget. He had to face conditions that were not entirely of his responsibility. He has been Minister of Finance for the last nine months only of the fiscal year which closed a month ago. However, as to previous budgets, the Minister of Finance must bear his share of responsibility as a member of the government for


some years past in relation to the shortcomings of previous budgets and the effect they have had in creating the type of situation with which the Minister of. Finance found himself confronted when preparing his budget proposals introduced in this house a month ago.
May I say that we are looking forward to a vote this afternoon upon the amendment to the amendment. As the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) is quite in keeping with the policies that have been set forth in this house on behalf of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, we of the official opposition intend to give our support to that amendment.
In the approach to any budget some fair and proper questions to ask ourselves are these:	What is the principle of the budget?
What does it seek to accomplish? What are the principal features of the problems that it envisages and what is the general nature of the solutions that are offered? If one submits the present budget to that type of scrutiny, one will find oneself unable to find a clear answer. The fact is that this is not a clear budget. It has no clear view of the problems of the day and consequently it has no clear-headed approach to them.
This is a budget without any pattern. This is a budget that is not founded upon any principle. So far as the minister's comments upon it are concerned, it is a budget that proceeds from one denial to another. His comments upon it were all of a negative nature. It is not dictated by Keynesian economics; it is not intended to meet the problem of unemployment; it is not this and it is not that.
After the closest examination of the budget and of the minister's comments upon it, one can only conclude that this budget is the product of muddled thinking, confusion, indecision and fear on the part of the government to admit the existence of problems with which the taxpayers and the people of this country are all too familiar. It was therefore highly proper that The Economist in its issue of April 19, in a letter from its Ottawa correspondent, should make this observation upon the budget:
On the assumption that Canada needs some stimulus to get back to its proper rate of expansion after last year's modest setback, this financing of tax cuts out of deficit is easily defensible. The budget speech in fact made it perfectly clear that this was the intention. But the government refuses to say so explicitly. It has never admitted that anything was wrong with the Canadian economy that required artificial stimulus, and it will not do so now. It would rather do good by stealth. The result is to leave it without any logical defence of the plunge into deficit financing.
Hence we have an approach to problems based not upon the admission of the existence

of problems but upon stealth. So this budget has no pattern and it has no principle; indeed, it is neither flesh nor fowl nor good red herring.
What are to be the effects of this budget? We do not know, Mr. Speaker, because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) will not tell us what were the intended effects of it. But we have had some interesting observations upon it. Mr. J. H. Perry, director of the Canadian Tax Foundation, in a speech last week on this budget, made this comment on the deficit financing that has now appeared:
While some have interpreted it as a shot in the arm for the economy, I would say it is more in the nature of a pink pill.
As I remember the purpose of pink pills, Mr. Speaker, they were for pale people. But the government makes no admission.
It is not unrealistic that we should look for some title for this budget. In the past we have had budgets that have been characterized in history by certain names. We have and many others. I suppose it would not be unfair to label this budget as "the budget of crumbs". That is the true measure of the size of the niggardly reductions which have been made in taxes. These niggardly reductions are the crumbs that have been permitted by this government to fall from its table;
I refer to the table of the swollen government treasury. In these trumpeted reductions we see certain facts that bring them into true focus and perspective.
Just what is in these income tax reductions? Here is this great reduction trumpeted as a reduction of 13-3 per cent. The married man, on an income of $3,000 per annum, with two children who receives this maximum reduction gets a total reduction this year of $7 in his income tax, and $14 in a full year. That is a reduction of 2 cents a day to him this year, and 4 cents a day next year.
These reductions, Mr. Speaker, are too small to give any material encouragement to enterprise in this country. Then with resort to a typical government device-that is, typical on the part of this government-these reductions have been postponed to July 1. In referring to that matter, the Minister of Finance spoke about this postponement as being usual. It is usual in the case of this government. They have had resort to this device in the past, making people think they were receiving bigger reductions than the budget actually brought about.
What was needed in relation to the income tax this year was a boost to initiative. What was needed was also a frank look at the present exemptions which, as the minister himself admitted in a speech some months 50433-215
The Budget-Mr. Fleming ago, are too low; and at the rates of taxation which, also by his admission, likewise are too high.
Second, what shall we say about this slight reduction in the corporation tax? It has been attacked by the C.C.F. in the course of this debate. They do not realize-or if they do so, it is no part of their wish-that the function of profits in the kind of economy we have, namely a free economy, is to provide the capital with which new plants, new jobs and new opportunities are created. That is the function of profits and capital in our economy. If you go on depriving people of the fruits of their labours and of their risks, you just blunt incentive, and the result is loss of opportunity and contraction in the number of jobs.
In recent years in this country we have seen a system whereby the government has been taking half of all the profits corporations have made. As I heard one government minister say in a speech in Montreal several years ago, the government is a 50 per cent partner in every Canadian corporation. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that it is a partner in the sense that it reaches in its long hand and abstracts from the treasury one-half of all the profits of every corporation in Canada. But in the sense that this is a profit and loss system and having regard to the fact that every one of these corporations that are talked about is capable of earning a loss as well as a profit, the government of course has no part in that aspect of its business.
However, it is interesting to see how the C.C.F. are at variance in this regard with Mr. Mosher, the president of the Canadian Congress of Labour. In a recent speech Mr. Mosher had this to say:
We have no alternative but to ensure sufficient profits to keep industry in motion, or be faced with unemployment, resulting in lower standards of living for a larger proportion of the workers.
I wish that hon. members of the C.C.F. would take to heart those words of Mr. Mosher. Then he went on to express the hope that "these words of common sense"- and indeed they were words of common sense -"would help to give recognition to the obvious fact that employers and employees are interdependent". That is a common-sense observation by Mr. Mosher, the truth of which has apparently never yet dawned upon those who mould the thinking and speaking of the C.C.F.
There is one thing I wish the minister had done with regard to corporation profits. I wish he had grasped the opportunity he had to encourage smaller businesses by enlarging the total permissible income on the part of those who qualify for the lower rate. Twenty

The Budget-Mr. Fleming thousand dollars is not enough in the way of permissible net earnings for a corporation to be entitled to the 20 per cent rate instead of the 47 per cent rate of taxation. The minister had there an opportunity to help small businesses in Canada, but he has allowed it to slip through his fingers.
But, sir, after this review of the vaunted reductions that have been made in the budget, let us in fairness realize this, that the minister has given to the people of Canada something that is going to help them so greatly to bear the burdens that he has laid upon them, help that will make them rather bear those ills they have than fly to others that they know not of. What has the minister given to the people of Canada to lighten the load? Sir, he has given them advice, and this is the advice that the minister has contributed to the suffering Canadian taxpayer. On February 21 he suggested that "Canadians accept in good humour the heavy taxes I have to impose". What a contribution to easing the burden of the Canadian taxpayer! The minister recommends that the Canadian taxpayer accept these heavy and excessive burdens with good humour. What a contribution to lightening the burden of the taxpayer!
This is the principal contribution of the budget to that end. I suppose it is in application of this new government panacea that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) has been going about the country making both his humorous and not so humorous observations. However, the Minister of Finance has given a new imposition, a new directive. The new imposition from the government that is dictated to the Canadian people is good humour in the acceptance of these burdens. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition think on the contrary that a sense of tax consciousness and tax resistance on the part of the Canadian people is a much healthier panacea for this government to face. It is only a strongly aroused sense of tax resistance on the part of the Canadian people that is going to drive the government opposite to measure up to its responsibilities to husband the resources of the Canadian people and not to inflict upon them unwarranted impositions.
As to the deficit, the minister hardly owned the poor thing. It had no part apparently in relation to any policy of the government. I call to mind a remark that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made on his return from Europe on December 29 when he said: "I wouldn't say a small deficit would be calamitous, but I think it's better to balance the budget." Sir, at least there is a statement of government policy, better to balance the budget, but we have had no explanation from the Minister of Finance as to why on tMr. Fleming.]
this occasion he felt it wise to depart from the only semblance of a statement of government policy in this regard that has recently come from any minister of the government.
But, sir, this budget is built upon an assumption. The whole basis, the whole foundation upon which the minister has constructed this budgetary edifice has been hope. We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition share the hope that the Canadian economy will be prosperous and strong, that it will expand this year, that there will be more prosperity this year than there was last year, but we do not think the minister should escape criticism for going about the building of his budget upon assumptions that do not seem to have much more relation to present reality than do the comments that have come from the government from time to time during the session in relation to the problem of unemployment. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that this year the Minister of Finance is assuming that the gross national product will be between 5 and 6 per cent more than it was in 1954; in other words, the gross national product will be $25J billion or more in 1955 and, as he himself says, "on that figure I shall base my revenue forecasts".
Let it be remembered that corporation profits in 1954 were 6 per cent smaller than they were in 1953. Let us remember that there was a disastrous decline in personal savings in Canada in 1954. At page 2777 of the appendix to Hansard of April 5 we have this statement:
. . . personal saving, or the amount set aside from current personal income, constituted 6'8 per cent of disposable income in 1954 compared with 9-2 per cent in 1953. In absolute terms personal saving fell from $1,539 million in 1953 to $1,137 million in 1954, a decline of $402 million, of which about half represented a reduction in saving in the form of farm inventories. The growth in personal assets was even more sharply reduced in 1954 than the $402 million reduction in personal saving would indicate: for personal saving takes many forms and involves changes in both assets and liabilities.
The trade outlook has a definite bearing on this question. Last year Canada slipped from third place, the proud position she had held for several years past in world trade, to fourth place, with Germany passing her and entering third place. In our current account on international transactions Canada had an unfavourable net balance of $427 million in 1954 and, notwithstanding a very slight improvement, we still had a trade deficit with the United States of $600 million. I am not going further into the subject of trade now. My leader will be speaking tomorrow and will deal in larger measure with this subject, but I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that in the face of these incontestable facts the minister goes

blithely ahead and bases all his calculations upon a very optimistic assumption.
Indeed, the minister gave some warning of his approach. Apparently he has been living in very close company with the Minister of Trade and Commerce for he said at Regina, as reported in the press of September 13, that "Canada's economy has nowhere to go but up." Yet at the very time he was making that statement all the figures indicated that the Canadian economy was going down. There was some improvement towards the end of the year but that came later.
We are faced with the unhappy fact with respect to agriculture in Canada today that farm cash income was down in 1954 to $2,378 million, a reduction of 14-3 per cent compared with 1953 and a reduction of 16-5 per cent compared with 1952.
We still have this vast problem of marketing our wheat, and until we do succeed in marketing our wheat in greater quantities it is simply idle for the Minister of Finance to go ahead and base budgetary plans upon optimistic and rosy assumptions of the kind he has made.
I wish to turn now to the subject of the problems that the budget has not touched, and there are many of them. Indeed, one could spend considerable time discussing problems that have been conveniently overlooked by the Minister of Finance and the government in the preparation of the budget.
The first is the problem of the sales and excise taxes. The fact is that this is a problem on which the minister has turned his back. If he was looking for a chance to help all the Canadian people, why did he ignore the sales tax? His predecessor had this to say about taxes on commodities in a speech I found recently which he made in Toronto a year ago. He made it a couple of weeks after presenting his budget, and here is what he said about the reductions he then proposed in the excise tax:
However, it appeared to me that some tax reduction was both possible and desirable. During the balance of the fiscal year, the tax reductions proposed in the budget will reduce taxes by about $36 million. When I came to consider just where tax cuts should be made, I decided, both for reasons of equity and of economic effects, that the bulk of the possible tax reduction should be in the commodity tax field.
Note these words, sir.
And that way, the tax cuts would benefit most Canadians.
That was in April, 1954, two weeks after the minister had made his budget speech in the House of Commons. His conception of the way to spread the benefits of tax reduction was to make reductions in excise taxes, these indirect taxes-
The Budget-Mr. Fleming

speechtext: And that has been done this year in the income tax, too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Nonsense; that is nonsense.
The sales tax has been completely overlooked. The excise tax has largely been ignored in the minister's approach to the problem.
Here is the sales tax that this government has raised to 10 per cent, this tax that was denounced by the predecessors of hon. gentlemen opposite, in 1935, at the general election in that year. Mr. Mackenzie King went up and down this country and denounced the sales tax as "that iniquitous tax". And what did he do when he came to office? He raised the sales tax to 6 per cent, and later it was raised under the Liberal government to 8 per cent, and then again to 10 per cent.
Yes, that is the way in which the Canadian people are made to enjoy the benefits of tax increases on the part of this government. Now, what about this sales tax? What about the excise taxes that apply to commodities that are in common use? I turn back to an editorial that appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of August 6, 1935, in which that mouthpiece of the Liberal party and of this government referred to the sales tax as imposing- and these are the words the editorial used- "a fine for selling and buying." Yes, a fine for selling and buying; and that was at a time when the sales tax was at less than half its present rate. They have more than doubled it since that time. They have more than doubled the fine on buying and selling.
And those are the taxes that, apparently, they believe in continuing to apply and enforce. These taxes apply to many of the basic necessities of life. How can this government possibly justify continuing the application of a 10 per cent sales tax on clothing, on boots and shoes, on household furniture, and a number of other necessities? How can this government any more justify the imposition of its tax on, for instance, tea and coffee? A deputation waited upon the minister before his budget was brought down and showed him how, if he would remove the tax on tea and coffee, he could save the Canadian consumers $9 million a year. But to that plea the minister turned a deaf ear.
Oh, they made much of the removal of the luxury tax-because that is the guise in which it was introduced a few years ago- on tires for motor vehicles. They have made much of the reduction of the excise tax from 15 per cent to 10 per cent on motor vehicles. Well, what they have done, in the way they have gone about it-in leaving the tax at far too high a figure, and giving no benefit at all to those dealers who had a stocked-up inventory of motor cars-has been to bedevil
3396	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fleming the wholesale and retail motor car business in Canada today. Many dealers have large inventories. In fact, I suppose there is hardly a dealer in Canada today who did not have a swollen inventory of motor cars before this reduction came about. And the government proceeds upon the assumption that, because some dealers may have benefited from the imposition years ago of this luxury tax, this 15 per cent tax-at the time of the Korean budget-therefore they should take a beating now. Now, sir, that was four years ago. And, what is more, the people are not the same today; and they are taking a very serious beating in this respect. The government is not prepared, however, to do anything to meet the inventory situation. On they go, applying these indirect taxes. They like them.
The second problem which has been ignored by the government is the problem of unemployment. This problem has been discussed at length in this session, or I would seek to go into it at greater length today. But let me content myself, in this limited time, with making this limited observation on the subject, that the government throughout this session has observed a conspiracy of silence in regard to unemployment; and it has carried that conspiracy of silence into the budget. It is still running away from the problem of unemployment.
This budget does not meet, in fact it cannot even make the pretence of meeting or even assisting to meet, the problem of unemployment. The government is still running away from that problem; they hope to ignore it. And only last Friday in this House of Commons we heard the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) running away from the promises the government made in 1945. Those promises that were made in 1945, that the federal government would assume the responsibility of providing for the unemployed employables-those promises, those undertakings, were most indecently interred here last Friday. The Prime Minister may think he can bury the proposals of the green book of 1945 in that indecent manner. But there are more recent phrases which will dog his political footsteps as long as time shall last, and they are his own words uttered in Quebec last September when he said this:
We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent. '
And we say to the Prime Minister, "Out of thine own mouth hast thou condemned


thyself, and not only thyself, but condemned thy colleagues as well".
This is a problem that is national in scope. It is beyond local responsibility. What we want on the part of this government, and what we still look for, are employment measures, some constructive and some effective approach to meeting the deterioration in the economic condition and the unemployment situation in Canada today.
The third problem this budget ignored is that taxes in Canada are far too high. In 1954 the total taxes imposed upon the Canadian taxpayer, whether dominion, provincial or municipal, aggregated something over $7 billion, a record sum. And, sir, of course the lion's share of this was taken by the federal government. I am thinking at the moment of the over-all problem. In 1929 figures show that 13 per cent of the gross national product of Canada went in taxes. In 1939 the figure was 16 per cent, and in 1955 it was 29 per cent of the gross national product. And of course there is an infinitely larger gross national product today. I say this is an unwarrantably heavy imposition upon the Canadian people, and that it has tended to reduce initiative at a time when the Canadian producer is facing keener competitive forces than have been faced for many, many years.
The fourth problem this budget does not meet is the problem of centralization, a problem created by the deliberate policy of this government to concentrate all taxgathering here at Ottawa. The dominion's proportion of the total revenue pie in Canada, placed upon the backs of the taxpayer, has doubled, in percentage, since pre-war days. This has got to the point now where it remained for a Liberal premier, Premier Hicks of Nova Scotia, in a speech he made on March 1, referring to the concentration of taxgathering at Ottawa, to say this:
It is possible that if the present trends continue we may lose our federal system of government by default, and will have brought about a one-government state without the Canadian people ever having paused to decide if such a result is desirable.
Note the words "one-government state". That is the trend in the taxing policy of this government, so clearly discerned and described by a Liberal provincial premier.
The fifth problem the budget ignores is the problem of waste and inefficiency. Sir, the contempt of hon. gentlemen opposite

was heaped upon Progressive Conservatives in the general election campaign of 1953 because we said that expenditures could be reduced without the sacrifice of any essential public interest in Canada, whether in defence or otherwise. Well, after ridiculing us, since those days the government has reduced the expenditures on national defence. They were running then at about $2 billion a year. They are now to run at a rate of $1,700 million a year. What we said could and should be done has been proven to be possible, but what has the government done at the same time? Have they sought to observe economy, to eliminate waste and extravagance in other departments? No, they have not. There is still the same old attitude on the part of the government. They can do no wrong, and it is not the kind of attitude that makes for efficiency on the part of those who serve under them.
There is still far too much water in the estimates that the government brings down before this house, and we shall continue to condemn this government for the deliberate way in which they endeavour to thwart and frustrate our efforts to squeeze some of that water out of those estimates. It is a known fact. The Auditor General has told us in the public accounts committee in previous years that there is a padding in all those estimates that runs to at least 5 per cent and sometimes 10 per cent. But let opposition members, as was done recently in the committee on estimates, in reviewing the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, try to reduce those estimates by 5 per cent, to eliminate that cushion, to squeeze the water out of the estimates, and what happens? The government opposite rallies its forces to defeat such a motion and preserve the water in these estimates.

Well, I am afraid the minister has not yet gone very deeply into the estimates. This is just a sample. The minister who has made this interruption is as good as any minister of this government. He has just said that he does not know of any water in the estimates. The fact of the matter is that apparently the existence of the water in the estimates is something that has escaped the notice of every minister, has escaped the attention of the government opposite, because they have no measures for squeezing the water out of the estimates, and so the waste goes on.
The Budget-Mr. Fleming
Although we are supposed to be having some regard for economy, the total numbers in the civil service increased by 10,000 from October, 1953, to October, 1954. Now, there are many civil servants who are not being adequately paid for their services. But, sir, it will take more proof than the government has given that increasing its numbers is the way to meet the problem of the civil service.
The sixth problem ignored by the minister in this budget is the succession duty. The succession duty act is crying for revision. On April 6, 1954, in his budget speech Mr. Abbott said at page 3733 of Hansard: "Our succession duty act is in need of revision." Then he pointed to efforts that had been made to revise other taxation legislation and said that he had asked the officials of the three departments concerned, finance, national revenue and justice, to commence work on rewriting the law and that he would hear representations. We were led to expect that within a year a new bill would be brought down, but now we are told by the present minister that he has not completed this work, and we have to wait another year for any approach whatever, even the simplest revision of this statute which is crying for revision today.
Seventh, this budget ignores the problems of the provinces and the municipalities. I point particularly to the fact that the budget makes no provision for reduction in the sales tax on goods purchased by municipal corporations or boards of education. Whatever, for example, our boards of education across Canada purchase that is subject to sales tax bears a double burden. It is paid for by the municipal and provincial taxpayers but the federal government comes along and loads another burden on them in the form of the sales tax.
Eighth, the government has ignored the problem of the welfare organizations, which have been pleading for remission of the sales tax on purchases made by them of goods for use in their work.
Ninth, the budget ignores the special problems of certain depressed industries, such as textiles, electrical goods and others.
Tenth, it has not faced the problem of providing exemption for pension contributions of recognized groups of self-employed persons.
Eleventh, it has not grappled with the silly way in which the finances of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are handled today
3398	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fleming by farming out to them the total yield from the indirect taxes on the sales of television sets and tubes and radio receiving sets and tubes.
Twelfth, it has not dealt with the problem arising from the fact that more money is taken from the people of Canada in deductions at the source from wages and salaries than is justified, and more than half of the taxpayers of Canada today are obliged to apply for refunds as a result of overpayment of taxes. It is time that problem was faced.
Thirteenth, the government has not met the problem of seizure of property and attachment permitted under taxing acts, as the government today arrogates to itself procedures that go far beyond the normal legal methods of recovery.
Fourteenth, the minister, while he acknowledged the problem of complicated provisions in our Income Tax Act, in a speech he made some months ago, has so far taken no note of that problem. We shall await with interest in that respect his bill to amend the act.
Fifteenth, the government has not dealt beyond this past year with the problem of the deficit in the old age security fund. We are still going along from hand to mouth, continuing the pretence that it is a contributory scheme. These are fifteen of the shortcomings of the budget.
In conclusion I wish to say that in so far as the proposed royal commission is concerned, a commission, as the minister described it, "to survey the future economic prospects" of our country, while we have no objection whatever to the appointment of a royal commission for this purpose, we do recognize that the selection of the personnel will be made by the government, and the success of this inquiry will largely depend upon the selection of the personnel. In any event, the task that has been assigned to the royal commission will be no substitute for action on the part of the government to meet immediately the pressing problems. There is one kind of inquiry that the commission might well have been asked to make, and that is the inquiry for which we have been asking for years, into the efficiency of government.
And so, sir, we have a budget which can only be described, it seems to me, as a budget of crumbs. It has turned its back upon and ignored pressing Canadian problems. It will be the duty of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to continue to press for remedy and redress


for the Canadian people in the face of those burdens that the government continues to load upon them.
