The reason we have emphasized the fact that the minister's income tax reductions amount to so little for the taxpayer in the
3400	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Knowles lower brackets and so much for the taxpayer in the upper reaches is that we feel this was the wrong way to do it. It is the minister himself who decides that he can afford a certain amount of money for income tax reduction. He says that the reduction he is going to make so far as personal income taxes are concerned will amount to $128 million in a full year or $85 million in 195556. He has said also that the reduction he is making in the corporation tax will amount to $43 million in a full year or $28 million in 1955-56. Those two tax abatements alone- never mind any others which are provided for in the budget-amount to $171 million in a full year or $113 million in 1955-56.
It is our contention that that full amount of $113 million in 1955-56, or $171 million in a full year, should have been made available to those in the lower income brackets. There are various ways in which that could be done, but mainly there are two ways. One way in which it could be done would be to raise the present exemption levels which are now $1,000 single and $2,000 married to figures such as $1,500 single and $3,000 married. At the same time it would be necessary-this is what we advocate-to increase the rates of taxation in the upper brackets. If you merely raised the exemption levels you would be giving more to the wealthy than you would to those in the lower brackets. If one is going to change the exemption levels, which is what we advocate should be done, it would call for a revamping of the rates for the various brackets, particularly those in the upper reaches.
Another way in which some of this $113 million in 1955-56 or $171 million in a full year could have been made available to those in the lower brackets would be by a reduction or elimination of the sales tax. It is our contention that when a government is supposedly concerned over the great masses of the people and has some money that it can throw in as a tax abatement it should arrange its budget so that that money accrues to the benefit of those who need it most and not those in the upper brackets. For example, a person drawing $30,000 a year does not need another $554 a year, as is shown in the table which I have placed on Hansard, but those in the $2,000 and $3,000 brackets do need whatever improvement in their economic position, whatever improvement in their standard of living, it is possible for the minister to provide in his budget.
I know as we all do from our experience here that the chances of getting a change in the budget once it has been announced are next to nil in the session in which such 

changes are proposed, but statesmen are always looking to the future, and of course all of us are statesmen when budget matters are under discussion. We are speaking to the minister having in mind next year's budget or perhaps the one the year after that. I suppose it is possible that the budget in the year after next may be an election budget, or perhaps next year's budget will be an election budget. Taxpayers generally are always glad to see elections because they do seem to have their effect on budgets.
Whenever that time comes I hope the minister will give the greatest amount of consideration, not to those in the upper income brackets who do not need assistance but to those in the lower income brackets who need far more in the way of improvement in their economic position and in their standard of living than is provided by a weekly tax reduction of 7 cents or 26 cents as provided by the minister in the budget now before parliament. I plead as strongly as I can that the minister in future budgets should think not of those who do not need assistance but rather of those who do.
There is another matter on which I should like to comment for a moment. That is with reference to the announcement made by the minister in his budget speech, as indicated on page 2740 of Hansard for April 5, 1955, when he said:
The government intends, therefore, to appoint a royal commission with instructions to look ahead and examine carefully our future economic prospects.
Mr. Speaker, I join with those who have welcomed the announcement of this royal commission. I hope it will be set up at an early date and that it will enter upon its work in the confidence that the findings it brings down will be implemented in an attempt to improve the general well-being of the people of this country. I think I might be pardoned for putting on Hansard at this point, in close relationship to the announcement of the minister which I have just read, this notice of motion of mine, which appears on the order paper where it has been since March 17 of this year. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the setting up of a 100th anniversary committee, with provision for participation by representatives of the federal and the provincial governments, for the purpose of planning the economic and social development of this country on a vast scale, including housing, slum clearance, conservation, irrigation and power projects, highway construction, the elimination of grade crossings, the building of hospitals, assistance to municipal projects, other public works and the strengthening of the economy of every section of the country; and that consideration should be given to the advisability of such a program being launched immediately and being pursued vigorously year by year so that on July 1,

1967, the people of Canada will be in a position to celebrate this nation's 100th birthday not only with fireworks and speeches but by the achievement of a land of health and abundance for all our people.
I shall	allow those who	may	read theminister's	announcement on	the	one	handand my proposed resolution on the other to note the interesting similarity. I earnestly hope this	royal commission	will	be	giventerms of reference that will	enable it	to do
a good job of research and that on the basis of its findings we will pursue vigorously a program of development for the health and well-being of this country and all our people.
I have just mentioned in my statement with regard to the future of Canada the question of health, and I should like to devote the remaining section of my remarks today to that question, arising in particular out of a question and answer, to be found in Hansard of Friday, April 29, 1955, on the orders of the day. The exchange is recorded on page 3289 and is as follows:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a
supplementary question of the Prime Minister? In view of his statement as to the greater weight that attaches to the views of the government of Ontario than attaches to that of some of the smaller provinces of the country, will he say that in view of what happened on Tuesday and Wednesday we are now closer to a nation-wide health insurance program than we were at the beginning of this week?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know how much closer we are to a nation-wide health program than we were before Tuesday and Wednesday, but very close attention is being given to the cost of that kind of a program.
Though I am one who deplores the long delay in connection with this matter of health insurance, I must say that I was glad to get that reply from the Prime Minister and I am glad to know that he is involved in a commitment that close attention is being given to the cost of a program of health insurance.
I call on the government to proceed with this matter now with much greater vigour and expedition than has been the case for the past 36 years, since it was first written into the Liberal platform in 1919. I believe that some progress was made in this building last week. I am speaking now of the cause of health insurance, not of the fortunes of any one political party, my own or any other. Previous to last week it seemed to me that Canada was more or less up against a brick wall so far as health insurance was concerned. My hon. friend, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), some months ago on the radio in the "Farm Forum" program, and more recently on television in a press conference program, had something to say about the possible need of a constitutional amendment-
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For a certain kind of plan.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-the possible need of a constitutional amendment for a certain kind of plan of health insurance. I think I know the kind of distinction that the minister had in his mind and still has. But I think he also muddied the waters by saying that, if a constitutional amendment were required, that would make necessary the agreement of all ten provinces. He did not say that all ten provinces had to agree before we could arrange to have a plan of health insurance in some of the provinces, but he did say that all ten would have to agree to the constitutional amendment if the plan to be put into effect were of a certain kind. I know the distinction, and I could discuss it at length, but that would simply take up my time. I know the distinction between a national health insurance plan and a nation-wide insurance plan. Some may think it is a distinction without a difference, but it is there and I realize that it is real.
My point is that, with the Minister of National Health and Welfare saying that kind of thing and with this question being kicked about from one election to another and being the subject of political speeches made in various quarters, it looked as though we were up against a brick wall. It seemed to me-and I shall speak quite frankly about it-that the federal government, with these references to unanimity or the fact that more than two or three of the provinces had to agree, was relying on the fact that the two central provinces would not agree and that therefore nothing would be done.
Quite honestly, I was afraid that they had some reason for that sense of reliance. It looked as though neither of the large central provinces of Canada was interested in this question, but last week, when the federal-provincial conference was held in the railway committee room, not far from where we are now in session, we had rather a surprise. The premier of Ontario joined other premiers who have already indicated an interest in health insurance by being actually the first one at that conference to ask that a study of a nation-wide health insurance program be put on the agenda for the meeting which is now to be held on the 3rd of October of this year.
I could make some political comments about the suggestion made by the premier of Ontario. We all know that there is an election campaign now on in Ontario, and maybe there is some connection, but even after the election is over, the fact of the matter is that Ontario has shown a definite interest in this question. Whatever party

The Budget-Mr. Knowles is elected on the 9th of June in Ontario, whether Conservative, Liberal or C.C.F., they all have health insurance in their platforms; so that whatever provincial government comes from Ontario to the federal-provincial conference here in October, it will be committed to carry through the expressed interest of the government of Ontario in a nationwide health insurance program.
I might interject at this point that no one is now suggesting that health insurance should be bureaucratically administered at the centre for every nook and hamlet in Canada. Everyone accepts the idea, laid down as a matter of fact in the 1945 green books, that it should be provincially administered. A growing number accept the principle that the responsibility of the government is to take those financial and other steps that will put the provincial governments in a position to carry through a program of health insurance, but the federal government simply has to meet that responsibility.
As I say, what took place last week is a matter that one could discuss at some length. It has many implications. It has many interesting political connotations. No doubt they will be discussed on the hustings in Ontario during the next four or five weeks. However, I think an objective summing up of what transpired last week must include the hopeful view that we made some headway; I refer to those of us who are interested in the cause of health insurance itself.
My main purpose in introducing this subject at this time is to call upon the federal government to be ready to give a lead in this matter in October. I am glad that the minister of health and welfare is paying me the compliment of being here and being interested in what I am saying. I hope that the federal government will be really ready, without any excuse, to lay before that conference on October 3 all the information that is necessary, on the basis of which this country might go ahead with a nation-wide health insurance program. It is my view that the federal government should take the lead, along the lines laid down in the green books of 1945, in making it possible for such provinces as are interested to get such a plan started. We now know that there are at least five provinces that are interested. There are four-British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland-that have hospital insurance of some sort and in some instances they are a bit further ahead. They are interested. Now Ontario has shown its interest. On that basis I think the federal government should take this matter as one of the most serious questions to be dealt with at the conference which will be convened on October 3.

I hope it will not be said at any point that between now and then there is not time to get all the necessary information together. If that is said by anyone, I am sure it will not be by the Minister of National Health and Welfare because I am sure he will remember that quite a while ago, on June 20, 1947, as recorded at page 4423 of Hansard of that year, he said this:
I can only repeat that we are engaging the full time of at least six persons in the department, with four additional persons who have other duties to perform. When we have the type of conference with the provinces which we envisage we shall be prepared at that conference to submit details in respect to the studies we have been making and are making and to bring about at the earliest possible moment the realization of a health insurance scheme.
I suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that if in June, 1947-nearly eight years ago-he could stand in this house during the course of the consideration of his estimates and say that his officials were ready with the details to make it possible to bring about at the earliest possible moment the realization of a health insurance scheme, they have infinitely more information now than they had then. The minister knows how highly we in this house think of the staff he has in his department. He not only is favoured in that he has two deputy ministers; he has two of the topmost civil servants in the federal government, namely Dr. Cameron, the deputy minister of health, and Dr. Davidson, the deputy minister of welfare.
In that department he has many other officials who really are most able and most efficient. He has a research department headed up by Mr. Willard, the staff of which really knows what is going on in the field of health insurance as well as in all the fields in which this department is interested. He has as director of the health grants program and of health insurance studies an outstanding man in the person of Dr. Jackson, who came to the service here from my province of Manitoba. I could go on with other names, and the minister has them in his mind too. He really has a good staff for getting together the information and for working out the details that could fulfil what he promised in 1947, namely that the federal government would be ready when a conference was held. It is going to be held now. It is eight years later. I am sure that the minister is ready.
Perhaps I should not take too long with these references, but on March 19, 1952, as recorded at page 586 of Hansard, there is a lengthy reply to questions that were put on the order paper with regard to progress made by the government since the previous session in health insurance studies and surveys in Canada. It is a lengthy and interesting reply

showing the attention then being given to this subject. Likewise, on Friday, January 22, 1954 the minister tabled sessional paper 84-A in reply to certain questions of mine in which I asked if the department had any papers, memoranda, studies, et cetera, regarding health insurance in other countries and any material relating to any possible program of health insurance in Canada. The reply was a long list on more than two sheets of foolscap paper, giving just the titles of many documents and memoranda on this question that had been prepared in the department. I myself have copies of some of them, and I can vouch for their usefulness and the thoroughness with which this work has been done.
My fifth question in the series that brought forth this sessional paper was this one:
What use is the government now making of this material?
The reply was:
This material is constantly being studied by senior officers of the department.
Similarly on Wednesday, May 5, 1954, the minister tabled sessional paper No. 84-D in response to certain questions of mine also on health insurance and on discussions with the provinces. This is a lengthy one. I will just read one question and answer. The question was:
Have there been consultations with the provinces concerning a program of health insurance?
The answer was:
Yes, at each meeting of the dominion council of health composed of the federal and provincial deputy ministers of health. Advantage has also been taken of frequent meetings of provincial ministers of health and welfare with the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare. In addition there have been consultations with certain provincial premiers.
In other words, across these years which have involved a delay that some of us have deplored, it is nevertheless true-and I will pay my compliment to the minister and his officials for it-that work has been done on this important question.
Mr. Speaker, if this government felt that in 1944 it could have a committee lay on the table of this house a draft bill entitled "The National Health Act", copies of which were printed and of which a certain use was made in 1945 as well, I submit that the government is far more ready today than it was then. Yet 11 years ago there was this draft bill of 43 pages which I hold in my hand, with most of the detail of a national health act, including health insurance grants, all spelled out. My copy is getting a bit yellow. I suppose the government cannot find its copies. But the main thing is not necessarily the resurrecting of this document of 11 years ago but
The Budget-Mr. Knowles rather the doing of something definite when this conference meets this fall.
My plea to the government is that when the conference meets, Mr. Frost be taken at his word and more. He asked for studies. I say this to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Give him more than studies. Or if Mr. Frost is not back here, and it is somebody else instead-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He will be back.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-you will find co-operation from the other possible premiers as well, because I believe that the people of Ontario and the people in the country generally are asking for and are anxious to have a real lead in this matter of nation-wide health insurance. I know that one of the tests so far as the great man of the Liberal government is concerned, namely, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), was spelled out according to a report in the Ottawa Citizen of June 24, 1953, when he said this:
A Liberal government will introduce a sound, workable national health insurance scheme in due course, just as soon as it can be done without placing an undue burden on the Canadian people.
The story goes on to point out, and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) did so as well in the summer of 1953, that this would be done when it was clear that the people of Canada want it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend is quoting the Prime Minister now. He knows that I have placed the statement of the Prime Minister on Hansard, and I think he ought to be very exact in what he attributes to the head of the government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I confess I am not able at the moment to find that in the Prime Minister's statement, and if I have misinterpreted what the Prime Minister said I shall withdraw it so far as he is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will be found in Hansard of June 19 last.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I have it here. It is about half a column. But I am sure the Prime Minister would not disagree with the proposition that if the people of Canada want health insurance the Liberals would be prepared to bring it in. My contention is that the government should be giving a lead in this matter and should not be waiting forever only to come along when it is finally realized that every last person in the country wants it. It is now wanted by a large number of people in a large number of provinces in this country, and I urge that action on this matter be taken in October of this year. So often we rise in the house and, in the very

The Budget-Mr. Knowles nature of things, say that action should be taken as soon as possible. I am pinning it down to October.
When the conference meets I think the government should go further than just meeting Mr. Frost's suggestion of studies of health insurance. It should have the details ready to carry through with the kind of plan that was so well spelled out in the green book proposals of 1945. I remind the house, the minister and others that although the provinces and the federal government did not get together on the package deal in 1945 nevertheless the idea of health insurance was not dropped from the terminology of the government. As everyone knows, when Mr. King on May 14, 1948, announced the important health grants program he started off by saying:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house on government policy with respect to health services and health insurance.
Later Mr. King said:
These measures also represent first stages in the development of a comprehensive health insurance plan for all Canada.
There comes to my desk many an item which uses that very language. I have here the five-year report on the national health program put out by the Department of National Health and Welfare. On pages 1 and 2 there is a summary statement of the purposes of the program, and point (f) in the summary of the purposes of the program is "to lay sound foundations for health insurance". I received not long ago the report of the annual meeting of the board of evangelism and social service of the United Church of Canada. Beginning on page 13 I find a report of an address made at the annual meeting in Toronto in January of this year by Dr. Gordon E. Wride of the Department of National Health and Welfare. At that time he said:
. . . these measures represented the first stage in the development of a comprehensive health insurance plan for all Canada.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare will recall that a while ago he let me have, because I complimented him on it, a copy of a very interesting address he made at Carleton Place on Saturday, February 12, 1955. He referred in the text of that address to the announcement made by Mr. King in May, 1948 and concluded an important sentence with these words:
. . . and the eventual establishment of a nationwide system of health insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would you mind reading the whole thing so we will get the context? I have just forgotten it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would you give me the extra minute or two it takes to read it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, it is worth reading, I think.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: 1 agree. The whole speech was good.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, never mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Maybe the minister will enter the debate and read the whole speech. The sentence he wants me to read in full is this:
Nearly seven years ago, Mr. King announced to parliament a program of national health grants which had as its objective the immediate strengthening of provincial and local health services and the eventual establishment of a nation-wide system of health insurance.
My point is that I want "eventual" to be made synonymous with October, 1955, not any later. Earlier this session I took advantage of the very kind invitation of the minister to visit some of the laboratories in his department. The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor) and others went along. We enjoyed our visit and found it very interesting and useful. On the way we were given some literature about the work of the department. One of the items was a mimeographed document entitled "Canada's National Health Services". I find that the first of these services that is spelled out is the national health grants program, and again I read:
The purposes of the program are-
Then there is a long paragraph which ends with these words:
... to lay the foundation for health insurance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask if the hon. member for Winnipeg South and the hon. member who is now speaking found themselves fully agreed on this subject when they visited our department?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On the subject of health insurance I think the hon. member for Winnipeg South and the Winnipeg Tribune are about the only two in Canada who are still opposed to health insurance.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, I know the hon. member would not wish to misrepresent me, and the statement he has made now is not correct. He said that I and the Winnipeg Tribune are the only two in Canada not in favour of health insurance. I cannot speak for the Winnipeg Tribune but I can for myself, and I say that statement is not correct. I am in favour of health insurance, but not the type of health insurance the hon. member is in favour of. If he will permit me, I should like to ask him a question while I am on my feet. Does he not realize that Canada is a federal state, and that constitutionally the matter of health and health

insurance comes within the purview of the provinces? Would he not think, therefore, that the initiative at the conference in October should come from the provinces rather than from the federal government?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I accept the hon. member's statement of privilege. So far as the Winnipeg Tribune is concerned, I had reference to an editorial a few days ago in which that paper took issue with the very request Mr. Frost had made. So far as my hon. friend is concerned, I am glad to find out that, while he may be interested in a different type of plan than I am, basically he also wants to see health insurance. I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare will take note of that. It is now nearly unanimous.
I point out also that during the summer of 1953, when we were in the midst of an election campaign, there was an article on this question written by none other than Mr. J. A. Hume, Citizen parliamentary writer. We all know the accurate prophet Mr. Hume has become. He was able to foretell with uncanny accuracy the outcome of the federal election in 1953. He seemed to know pretty well last December or January what would be in the speech from the throne opening this session of parliament. He had some pretty good ideas as to what might be expected in the budget which was announced on April 5, and just a short while ago he predicted accurately the date of the Ontario election which has now been set for the 9th of June.
In the summer of 1953 this uncanny prophet, whose record for accuracy one must note, had this to say in an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen headed "Health Insurance First Liberal Aim":
Inauguration of a contributory national health insurance scheme during the life of the new 22nd parliament will shortly be announced by Prime Minister St. Laurent as the No. 1 objective of his Liberal administration if re-elected on August 10.
I am sure my hon. friends across the way will not want to disappoint Mr. Hume, let alone some 15 million other Canadians. I am sure they do not want to spoil his record as an accurate prophet, and I hope the point in the life of the twenty-second parliament to which Mr. Hume referred will be in October of this year, and that the government will really take action.
I have shown-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am obliged to advise him that his time has expired.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps I could go on for two minutes to make up for the time I spent
The Budget-Mr. Decore reading from the speech of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I had already made what I thought was a generous allowance for the interjection of the minister. But if the hon. member is accorded unanimous consent, then of course he may proceed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question before he takes those two minutes more? He has dealt, in some particularity, with the speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare before the 1949 election. It seems to me, however, that he overlooked a very important matter when he did not give us the speech or speeches made by the minister before the 1953 election. I think we can assume that they were made, and it would be important to have them on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To save the hon. member's time, because I realize his time is precious, may I say to the adventurous member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) that I shall be very glad to supply him with all the material which, obviously, he requires-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That saves me not two minutes but two hours, Mr. Speaker.
Just this in conclusion, let me thank the house for giving me the extra time. I have shown this front page of the Toronto Daily Star of May 15, 1948, to the house on a number of occasions, and I feel that perhaps I should apologize for bringing it down again today. It is almost worn out. However, I did bring it down because it does seem to me that today it is more appropriate than ever. Mr. Mackenzie King made his announcement of the health grants program on May 14, 1948. The next day the Toronto Daily Star ran this headline, "Can't Wait for Ontario-King".
I ask, Mr. Speaker, who is waiting for whom now? Ontario wants studies in the matter. The Minister of National Health and Welfare says he wants health insurance as soon as possible, as soon as we can afford it, as soon as all the difficulties can be ironed out. The people of Canada want it. I call for action, without fail, on this important question at the federal-provincial conference to be held on October 3 of this year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate some hon. members in the opposition have endeavoured to create the impression that Canadians in the lower income brackets did not get very much consideration by way of personal income tax reductions as compared with those in the substantially higher income brackets.

The Budget-Mr. Decore
I think a very good example of that type of thinking has been shown to us this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has just taken his seat. And I might add that if we were to examine the statement made by his leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), it would be clear that he follows the same line of thinking. I now quote from Hansard, page 2956, where the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the leader of the C.C.F. party, had this to say:
When we heard the minister we jumped to the conclusion that the reduction in the tax was more substantial in the lower brackets than in the higher income brackets. What the minister actually did, in spite of any impression to the contrary which was contained in the table which I looked at the night the budget was placed before us, was to reduce the tax rate by two percentage points in all personal income brackets.
This means that the married taxpayer with two children receiving family allowance and earning $3,000 a year gets a tax reduction of $7 for the whole of 1955.
Then he went on to say this:
The married man with two children receiving family allowances with an income of $100,000 a year will receive a tax reduction of nearly $1,000, or to be precise, $977. The higher the income the more rebate that is received.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave an example of the reduction for a person who has an income of $400,000 a year, and I believe he gave the reduction as $3,977.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps my arithmetic was not correct. I accept the hon. member's figure. In any event, in all fairness to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I would say that the figures they have given are correct. I think, however, that these same figures should be examined from a different angle, so we can get a better perspective and a better picture of the whole situation.
If we were to refer to table V at page 2737 of Hansard, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred, we might see what is stated there concerning the married man with an income of $2,300 and with two children, both of whom are eligible for family allowance. What happens to him? The fact is that this taxpayer does not receive any tax reduction at all. If I were to leave it at that, then of course I would be endeavouring to leave the same impression the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been trying to leave. But the reason this taxpayer has not received any reduction in personal income tax lies in the fact that he is not taxable at all. At the same time, in addition to his income of $2,300 this same


man receives family allowance cheques for his two children which, in the year, amount to something like $150.
Let us now turn to the man with two children and an income of $2,500. What is the tax he would pay in 1955? Of course when using the figures shown in table V one must add the 2 per cent old age security tax. It appears from the table that his tax in 1955 would be $28. Yet, at the same time this man who must pay the tax of $28 receives family allowance cheques from the people of Canada, through the policy initiated by this government, to the extent of about $150. In other words, in addition to his income of $2,500 he receives a bonus of approximately $120.
Let us take another figure that was used by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, who referred to the man with an income of $3,000 and with two children eligible for family allowance. His tax for the year 1955 would be $98. At the same time, by way of family allowance cheques he receives $150, which leaves him more than $50 to the good, by way of bonus, if one wishes to put it that way.
Family allowances were enacted to assist people with children in the lower income brackets, so those children may be better fed, better clothed and have better educational facilities; in general, to afford them better opportunities to become good citizens of this country. At the same time, one should take this into account. A young married couple with two children usually have to care for, or they have a moral obligation to assist, their fathers and mothers in their old age, when they reach the age of 65 or 70. Under the policy of the federal government these people in the lower income brackets are receiving indirect benefits from our social security measures in the form of old age security or old age pensions. I would remind this house that the government will spend approximately $1 billion in the coming year on our social security measures, which were intended to assist in particular those who require assistance, and those who are in the lower income brackets.
Let us again refer to table V to see what happens to a person who has an income of $100,000. speechtext:
It has been the policy of the present government for some years to tax people with high incomes to assist those in the lower income brackets. It is a form of distribution of wealth. The government also follows the policy of encouraging private free enterprise in order to induce people to take risks and to go into various business ventures. Despite our huge expenditures for defence purposes-and as we all know they amount to almost one-half of our total revenue-in this country we have one of the best social security programs of any comparable country in the world. It is also a fact-and if anyone wishes to challenge this I should like to hear him do so-that our rates of income tax are among the lowest in the world, and our personal exemptions for income tax purposes are the best in the world for people in the lower income tax brackets.
Having dealt with some of the criticisms that have been levelled against the government and the budget, I should now like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance and the government certain problems which exist, so the government may take the necessary steps to solve them. I have in mind a problem which is very real and very serious. It has to do with young men who wish to make a start in farming. I have made reference to this matter before, and I wish to do so again. Everybody knows that because of the increased value of farm land generally and the mechanization of farming which involves costly farm machinery, a young man who wishes to start in farming must have at least in the neighbourhood of $15,000.
Nearly all the young men who desire to go into farming in this country find that this amount of money is simply not available to them. It is true we have the farm loan act and the farm improvement act, which were intended to provide credit to farmers, but
The Budget-Mr. Hansell this credit is extended to farmers who already have land, who already have buildings and machinery. They may be able to borrow money from the farm loan board to buy more land or additional machinery, or to borrow for farming purposes under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, but there is nothing on our statute books to give assistance to young men who wish to start in farming.
It is my contention that those young men who have the experience, who have the knowhow and who desire to farm, should remain on the land. They should not go into the industrial centres seeking jobs when they are better qualified to remain on the land, because in so doing they merely add to the problem of unemployment. Therefore I ask the question, could not some scheme or some plan be put into operation to assist these young people and give them a start in farming? I do not pretend to have any formula, but I should like to draw attention to the National Housing Act. Under that act thousands and thousands of Canadians have been able to acquire houses which they otherwise would never have been able to acquire. They have been able to do so because there was a plan or scheme introduced by this government. In enacting that legislation the government did not take any risk, and the lending institutions did not take any risk. Thousands of people have benefited and thousands more will continue to benefit under the National Housing Act. Perhaps a similar scheme could be enacted along those lines for young men and women who wish to go into farming.
I believe that investment in land is the best investment one can make. Furthermore, we already have the machinery set up. The Department of Veterans Affairs offices in the various provinces in Canada have had some experience in this type of work. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture, and the cabinet to give this matter some thought. Probably they could appoint a committee or find some other means of solving this problem.

The Budget-Mr. Hansell when so many have preceded me. I have listened to about 19 budgets brought down by this government, and during that time have listened to the number of speeches which have been delivered this session multiplied by 19. I find it difficult to say much that is new.
The budgets we listen to every year are the same old budgets. There is no difference basically and fundamentally in any of them; they are all the same with respect to basic financial policy. The only shade of difference is that there may be a reshuffling of taxation. Some years some things are taxed higher than others, but the next year those same things may be taxed a little less. It is entirely a matter of running the country one year after another with no change in basic financial policy, but only a reshuffling of the mechanics of the same policy.
I am not going to attempt a detailed analysis of the financial aspects of the budget, as there are other members of the house who are more capable of doing that. Some of them have already tried to give evidence of their capabilities. I am not too much concerned with the analysis of budgets; I am not too concerned with what the financial wizards of the finance department have to say about things; I am not too much concerned about what the big boys of Wall street or of St. James street or of Bay street have to say; I am more concerned about what my friend Joe of Fifth street has to say. I am not too much concerned as to what big business or big industrialists may say about the budget, but I am concerned with one of two things, that is how it affects the rank and file of the people of Canada.
I do not know, but my experience is that these budgets are somewhat glamourized. Budgets come and budgets go, and somehow or other we bow down in humble obeisance to finance and surround it with all the dignity of great potentates and what have you. I always want to laugh when the financial critic of the Conservative party rises in the house and with an air of importance looks over at the finance minister and says, "May I ask the hon. Minister of Finance a question; can he inform us when we may expect the budget?" This happens every year. Then the minister rises; he does not tell him, he simply puts him off. Then perhaps a week or two later some front bencher will rise and ask the minister if he has given any further consideration to the date of the budget.
I do not think my friend Joe of Fifth street cares one bit about the date the budget is brought down. It is brought down eventually, and then another thing happens. Why people

should want to crowd into this house on budget night to hear the budget speech is beyond me. As a matter of fact we get telephone calls from our friends and other people wanting to know if they can get tickets to the galleries.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 22, to amend the Canada Grain Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the words of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the western farmer is fighting mad today, and he is fighting mad for a good reason. A fundamental right which he has enjoyed for over 50 years has been arbitrarily taken away. I refer to the right of the farmer to deliver grain to the elevator of his choice. This is the third successive year in which I have introduced this bill, which sets forth a method by which farmers may have restored to them the right to deliver grain to the elevators of their own choice. Canadians fought in two wars to protect democracy and to prevent the coercion of the few by the many. Thousands of western farmers today are asking that this fundamental right be restored to them.
Under the present system farmers have lost that fundamental right. As hon. members know, in periods of congestion elevators have been plugged. Farmers have been able to deliver grain only to those elevators that obtain the box cars, and they are able to deliver grain to a particular elevator only to the extent that that elevator company may obtain box cars. The railway companies and the government have in their hands the power to decide where and in what proportion farmers may be able to deliver their grain to the various elevator companies. Far too often railway companies going into a town with four or five elevators, ignoring completely the desires of the farmers as to where

they wish to deliver their grain, spot one box car to each elevator and therefore determine by that method the proportion of grain that will be handled by the various elevator companies.
Farmers and farm organizations of western Canada have been very patient indeed with this government. They believed that if they came to the minister and the government quietly, without publicity, and explained particularly to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in a reasonable manner their important and just demands, the minister would lend to them a sympathetic ear and that between them they would be able to find a method by which that fundamental right could be restored to western farmers. But, instead of getting a sympathetic ear, instead of getting action from the government, they have found that the government has ignored their requests. The government has turned a deaf ear and has said, in effect, "You shall not have restored to you the right to do your business with the elevator firm of your choosing".
I wonder how any cabinet minister or any member opposite would like to be told the business firm from which he must buy his automobile. How would any hon. member like to be told that he would have to take a Volkswagen if he wanted a Cadillac? I am sure he would resent it very much. I wonder if the wife of any hon. member opposite would like to be told that she must shop for her groceries at a certain store on a certain day, and at no other store, if she wants to eat and to feed her family. That in effect is what farmers have been told by this unfair and unjust method of box car distribution, namely that if they are to get any income at all in a given period of time in order to buy food and clothing for their families and for the purchase of farm supplies, they must deliver grain whether they like it or not to the elevator that has the box cars.
So I say that every hon. member opposite should support the measure I am now moving; and every member of parliament from the prairie provinces, if he is to carry out the wishes of his constituents, particularly if he represents a rural constituency, has no choice but to support the proposition that farmers right now shall have restored to them this fundamental right that has been so arbitrarily taken away.
I know that hundreds of letters come to my desk from individual prairie producers asking that this fundamental right be restored, and I know that my colleagues in
Canada Grain Act
this group are also receiving many hundreds of letters. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce must have received in his office many thousands of letters from wheat producers, and I would like to have the information as to just how many thousands of letters have come to the minister's office asking that this fundamental right be restored to the farmers. Is it 5,000 letters or
10,000	letters? Is the wheat pool now nearing its objective of getting to the federal government and to members of parliament a total of 30,000 letters asking that this democratic right be restored? I know the campaign has gone on very successfully during the past few weeks, and it is still going on.
I venture to say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has received more letters from western farmers on this subject in the last three weeks than any western cabinet minister has received since 1942, when farmers staged a march on Ottawa. In the words of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the farmers are fighting mad; they are out to get justice for themselves; and if the method of requesting the government by letter this time does not work, then they are going to adopt other measures until this right is restored. In that campaign they have the full and complete support of the C.C.F. party.
I am hoping that members of parliament on all sides of this house will vote for the measure that is before the house today. When I first moved this bill in the spring of 1953, Mr. Ross, the then member for Souris, speaking on behalf of the Conservative party, said that it was a step in the right direction. The Minister of Trade and Commerce then moved an amendment that the bill be given the six months' hoist, and the members of the Conservative party voted against that move by the government to kill the bill. Last year, however, the Conservative party in this house reversed its stand. I am going to issue a warning to the Conservative party right now that, if they wish to get any support whatever in rural areas of western Canada, they had better support the proposition that farmers be given the right to deliver grain to the elevator of their own choice. I am asking them to reconsider their stand and when the vote is taken to support this measure.
As I have said, the letters have come in by the thousand to members of parliament and to the government. I am sure I could not explain the desires and the wishes of western grain producers in this regard as well as

Canada Grain Act
they are explained in this letter from Mr. Harold E. Voechting, of Tribune, Saskatchewan, dated April 20, 1955, which reads as follows:
Mr. Hazen Argue, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Argue,
As our member of parliament for our riding, I follow with interest your various speeches and debates in the House of Commons.
As a farmer, grain grower, I am vitally interested in any legislation that is for better living and1 working conditions for the farmer. Grain quotas, box car shortage, and storage space are as you know one of our biggest headaches on the farm, and the unequal distribution of box cars is very annoying. Under the present system, if a farmer wants to sell any grain he must take it to the elevator that the railways see fit to send cars to. Special shipping orders by the wheat board have made the car order book obsolete. I think it is time some legislation was enacted to let the farmer at least have a choice of where he can deliver his grain. We are supposed to be living in the freest country in the world, yet our government will not devise a plan that will enable the grain grower to be able to deliver his grain to the elevator of his choice.
I urge you, Mr. Argue, as our very capable M.P., to do your utmost to have the government pass such legislation at this sitting.
That sets forth the wish of western farmers to have restored to them the right to deliver grain to the elevator of their own choice.
Government members may claim that the present situation is merely temporary, that if we should have another poor crop the congestion will not be nearly as great, and that therefore it is unnecessary to amend the Canada Grain Act in this regard. However, I should like to point out to government members that modern methods of harvesting our grain crops make it possible and practical for farmers to harvest all their grain within a few weeks, and haul it out to the elevators. The farmers being very short of cash, as they are particularly when their crop is small, are anxious to haul out as much grain as they can, as quickly as they can, in order to cover their accounts. Hence they naturally attempt to haul their grain out as quickly as possible after harvesting so that even if there is a relatively small crop, as there was in 1954, the congestion continues. The congestion that has continued over the last three years with regard to this box car situation is therefore likely to continue in the future, I suggest, because of our new, modern methods of harvesting and hauling grain.
That being the case, I suggest to the government that the amendment that is required is not one to amend the Canada Grain Act just for this year, to meet a temporary situation, but is an amendment that is necessary to meet a situation that is likely to continue for many years to come.
In this demand all farm organizations in western Canada are united. The western

wheat pools are speaking with one voice. The farmers' union, in one brief after another presented to the government, have mentioned the problem of box car distribution and have asked that a fair method of box car distribution be adopted. The measure I am proposing this afternoon is that the Canada Grain Act be amended to read as follows:
If, at any time, no unfilled application for a car appears In the car order book at a marketing point, the railway agent shall then apportion railway cars among the elevator companies in the proportion that the acreage has been divided among the elevator companies.
The bill in the preceding paragraph makes it possible for farmers to list their acreage and to apportion their acreage among the elevator companies at the marketing point. After they do that, as set forth in this bill, before October 1 in each year, then the number of acres allotted to each elevator shall be added up and, on the basis of the farmer's choice as outlined by the allocation of his acreage, the railway companies are accordingly required to apportion the box cars among the elevator companies.
As I have said, this fundamental principle is being supported by all farm organizations today. The Saskatchewan wheat pool has sent to the various members of parliament a brochure setting forth their opinions and their suggestions as to how this problem can be dealt with. They are asking that the farmer himself have the right, by posting his acreage, to elect where he wishes to deliver his grain and by so doing to make provision for box cars to be spotted accordingly.
The only real difference I can see between the bill that is now before the house and the proposition advanced by the western wheat pools is that by my bill the farmers would vote by open ballot, whereas the wheat pools are suggesting that the choice be made by secret ballot. If the government is prepared to adopt the suggestion of the wheat pool organization, I for one shall be pleased to support it. I do not think it makes much difference whether the farmer sets forth in his permit book, as he now does with regard to his seeded acreage, his opinion as to where he wishes to deliver his grain or whether, as the pools suggest, he expresses his opinion on a ballot which is subsequently placed in an envelope and sent to the board of grain commissioners for their guidance.
The thing that is important is the principle, namely that farmers have a right to deliver grain to the elevator of their own choice. Farmers, I believe, should have the same economic freedom as is now enjoyed by every other group in the Canadian economy.

By this bill we are asking that farmers in western Canada have that fundamental freedom restored to them.
I suppose that members from non-prairie provinces may say they do not take any interest in this measure. But I suggest that the principle involved in this measure is far more fundamental than whether a number of box cars should go to one prairie elevator or another. The extremely important principle is that no group of Canadians should be denied something that I suggest every member of parliament must believe is a democratic, basic Canadian right. The right is that any Canadian, when he decides to sell his produce-whether it be agricultural produce or whether it be his labour-has a right to sell that product to the firm of his own choosing. To say that western farmers today have that freedom would be to deny the truth of the statements by thousands of farmers that have been received by members of parliament and by the government.
The wheat pool set out in some detail the type of amendment they are seeking. In addition to this general, broad method of determining the distribution of box cars, they say that if the wheat board must order out of turn box cars, those additional out of turn box cars must also be calculated in the formula. I would suggest one further amendment that might be placed in the statute or might be provided for by regulation. That is if, because of the out of turn box cars, within the full year period the exact apportionment has not taken place according to the farmers' own wishes, whatever extra box cars an elevator may have obtained should be carried forward into the next year and be treated in the next year's formula. If that were done the apportionment could be made absolutely in keeping with the farmers' own wishes.
We have been at this problem now for a number of years. We expected that we would get it solved when the transport controller was appointed. The transport controller had his powers extended in the 1953-54 session. Under that statute the transport controller has power, in my judgment, to do everything that we are now asking be done in the way of the distribution of box cars. However, he has never cared to exercise the authority to allocate box cars that parliament has provided.
As I have said in previous debates, he does not really allocate box cars at all. If a member or someone else gets a complaint that a given point is not getting sufficient box cars, and if the transport controller is asked to do something about the situation, he will
Canada Grain Act
bring it to the attention of the railway company in the hope that the railway company will provide additional cars at that marketing point; but at no time does he allocate box cars among the elevator companies on the basis of the farmers' own choice.
To solve this problem we have tried the transport controller, and that has been a complete failure. The minister has said in the past that the car order book, a provision that has been in the Canada Grain Act for a great many years, was sufficient to give farmers the right to deliver grain to the elevator of their own choice. For example, in the debate on December 15, 1953, the Minister of Trade and Commerce had this to say, as found at page 937 of Hansard:
I do not think enough attention is being paid to the car order book.
Then he went on to explain the provisions of the car order book. He said the car order book is a method by which the farmers can determine where box cars shall be spotted, and by that method can provide for their use sufficient space in the elevator where they wish to market their grain. Of course the fallacy of that argument is that the car order book has already been tried. The car order book has a lot of merit and can do a job in many instances, but as soon as the farmers at a local marketing point have the car order book in effect, and as soon as other farmers at other marketing points across western Canada have the car order book in effect, what happens? The transport controller steps in, uses his wide powers and suspends the operation of the car order book. Farmers are then back in exactly the same position they were in before they began using the car order book.
In other words, instead of the transport controller and the government assisting the farmers to market their grain at the elevator of their own choice they have taken away in many instances the one provision which was placed on the statute books of the country long ago so the farmers might have that right. Instead of helping the farmers to use this fundamental right the government helped take it away.
We thought we were making some progress last year. We had a long discussion in the standing committee on agriculture. We had witnesses from the various grain companies. We had the minister saying that he was considering the implementation of a car cycle whereby the government, the transport controller, whoever was in charge, would take a period following the war in which there was little congestion, and on the basis of the business done by each elevator company at the marketing point would apportion box

Canada Grain Act
cars accordingly. I was never enthusiastic about that procedure. I thought something better should be done. I did not think you could obtain justice for the farmers in 1955 by tying the distribution of box cars to the dead past, to the wishes of farmers in a previous period even though it was a period in which there was little congestion. But I was quite prepared to admit that that kind of car cycle woud be a vast improvement over the present method of allowing the railway companies, in the main, to determine the distribution of box cars at any elevator point.
I have reviewed the lack of action by the government. I have pointed out the fact that the government, instead of helping the farmers to solve this problem whenever by their own volition they have attempted to do so, has permitted the transport controller to step in and block the farmers' action by cancelling the car order book.
I have said many times that the personnel of the board of grain commissioners are not carrying out the wishes of organized agriculture and the farmers generally. We all know that in some instances the board is loaded with straight political appointees, and if it is not a straight political appointment then you can almost be certain it will be somebody who was very closely connected with the Winnipeg grain exchange. Whenever you get this Liberal-grain exchange partnership the farmers of western Canada are bound to suffer. I think that is one of the real reasons why they are in this difficulty today. Apparently there is no one in the board of grain commissioners or in the ranks of the cabinet who wishes to restore to the farmers this fundamental right. They would far rather continue this conspiracy to deprive the farmers of a fundamental Canadian right.
I do not claim that this bill is necessarily the final answer. I do not really care whether or not this particular measure is adopted, as long as I get the assurance from a responsible cabinet minister that legislation will be brought in by the government at this session to fulfil the letter and the spirit of the requests of the three western wheat pools as far as amendments to the law are concerned. I am prepared to go further. I am prepared to support in committee any amendment by the government that they might think would improve the measure in order to carry out its principal objective. As a further alternative, if after the measure has received second reading, the government would like the whole question reviewed once again by the standing committee on agriculture and the bill reported back to the house at this session, I am quite prepared to agree.

But I shall not allow the measure to drop unless and until there is concrete assurance from the government that action will be taken at this session to meet the requests of organized agriculture. If the Liberal members from Saskatchewan wish to stay in tune, which is questionable, with the opinions of the Saskatchewan Liberal party, they will support the principle of this measure. But since Saskatchewan now has two Liberal parties, or a Liberal party that functions in two parts, it is rather difficult to forecast what their position may happen to be.

Resolutions designed to make life more enjoyable for farmers were passed at the provincial Liberal party convention here Friday.

Liberal members of the house from Saskatchewan can demonstrate that they really want to take steps that would make farm life in Saskatchewan more enjoyable, not by supporting a fundamentally C.C.F. measure but by supporting a resolution of their own convention in Saskatchewan last fall, calling for amendments to the Canada Grain Act to restore this fundamental right to western farmers.
To show that at least the provincial section of the Liberal party meant business, may I point out that a resolution was unanimously supported in the Saskatchewan legislature which asked that this right be restored. The resolution, moved by Mr. Wooff and seconded by Mr. Swallow, is listed in the votes and proceedings of the legislative assembly of the province of Saskatchewan for March 24, 1955, and reads as follows:
That this assembly urge the federal government to implement a box car distribution that insures the farmer the right to deliver grain to the elevator of his choice.
A debate arising, and the question being put, it was agreed to unanimously.
That was the resolution passed by the Saskatchewan legislature and agreed to unanimously by members of the Liberal party and of the C.C.F. party, asking the federal

government to implement a box car distribution system that would ensure to the farmer the right to deliver grain to the elevator of his own choice. It was carried unanimously; all were for it.
I ask Liberal members of parliament from Saskatchewan and from other provinces in western Canada to stand in their places and support the restoration of this fundamental right to western farmers.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about Bill No. 22. As the hon. member sponsoring the bill has said, this very same bill was presented to the house last year and the year before. Each year I have had quite a bit to say, and I do not propose this year to repeat what I said previously.
However, in view of statements made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), not to mention the gratuitous political advice he so profusely handed out to all members in the house, I should like to refer to some of his remarks. One thing that struck me above everything else is that he tried to leave the impression-indeed he so stated specifically and repeatedly-that the government had purposely gone out of its way to deny a long-acquired right of farmers to deliver to the elevator of their choice. Of course nothing could be more ridiculous than such a statement.

speechtext:
I shall. Just hold on. I have 40 minutes to prove it. Everybody knows that no one has denied anyone any right on that score at all. It just so happens that, because of a shortage of box cars, a situation has developed.
The hon. member said the government had ignored the plea and the demand of farm organizations out west. Again, to say the least, this is a very broad exaggeration of the true situation; because I am sure that even the farm organizations, particularly the three wheat pools primarily concerned with this matter, would be the first to deny that statement. On every occasion-and it was repeated recently-the government and the Canadian wheat board have given the matter careful consideration and have tried to meet the wishes of all concerned, including the private line companies, in order to find a solution to this problem.
One of the main difficulties of my hon. friend from Assiniboia is that he associates with this bill the right of a person to deliver to the elevator of his choice. I suggest there is a vast difference between the bill as he has presented it and the right to deliver to the elevators of our choice; because there are grave doubts in the minds of many producers in western Canada that this bill will do what the hon. member says it will do.
Last year, when we sat in the committee on agriculture, this whole matter was gone into at some length. Representatives of the pools were there to testify and the secretary of the line elevators' association, which represents all the line elevators in western Canada, was also present to give his testimony.
In this way we got the story from all angles, including evidence from the board of grain commissioners and the Canadian wheat board. As a matter of fact representatives of the various pools were asked what they thought of the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and each of them replied that he had very grave doubts that the bill could be made workable.
After listening to all the evidence and doing my share of study of this problem, it is my opinion that the bill is not workable and, as I said, I believe the pools agree. As a matter of fact, as the hon. member has said, the pools have offered another method by which they thought this situation might be resolved.

Now, the hon. member for Assiniboia suggests in one breath that we should adopt this bill today, and in the same breath urges that we should adopt the suggestion of the pools. I do not see how the two views can be reconciled.
